articles.title: Samsung's Frame Pro isn't just a gorgeous TV, it opened my eyes to art
articles.summary: The design-forward TV delivers a performance that few in the category can – while attracting compliments as wall decor. Can’t hear what’s playing on TV? It’s not your ears, it’s the flat screen. These affordable soundbars can help.
body: When they are screening blockbusters, huge TVs are cinematic portals to another world. When they’re off, huge TVs are hideous black mirrors. Samsung has always understood this home decor landmine and aimed to defuse it in 2017 with The Frame, the first-ever “art TV”: a television disguised as a framed painting.

As a female tech editor who spent years appraising the banal designs of 1990s tech, I can palpably remember how thrilled I was to see this innovative melding of form and function, which seemed like a novel luxury at the time. Fast-forward nearly a decade, and Samsung’s pricey niche concept has gone decisively mainstream, with competition from LG, Hisense, TCL and even Amazon.
But Samsung hasn’t been sitting still: The Frame Pro boasts cordless architecture, a matte screen and customizable magnetic bezels.
points: The design-forward TV delivers a performance that few in the category can – while attracting compliments as wall decor.

When they’re off, huge TVs are hideous black mirrors.

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: swot up with these lessons in back-to-school dressing
articles.summary: September is the most fun time of year to shop, but it can also be dangerously seductive. Keep your wits about you with these tips. I used to love back-to-school shopping when my children were little.
body: Luckily for me, you don’t have to grow out of back-to-school shopping even though your children do, because in fashion September is considered the start of the new year. This is eminently sensible, because this time of year is a much better moment for a restart than January. The actual new year is dark and bleak and makes resolutions and projects feel intimidating rather than exciting. But right now, the evenings are still light, and while I’ve still got a bit of a tan pretty much anything feels possible.

Back-to-school is a whole vibe, not just a shopping spree. The juice is in the back-to-school thinking, rather than the back-to-school shopping. It is about snapping back into focus, getting your head in the game. Life gets a little loose over summer, which is delicious, but sometime about now you get a restless itch for a new tempo: more coffee and less wine, more can-do and less can’t-be-bothered.

This is the most fun time of year to shop. I love seeing the swimwear and sandals swept away by crisp shirts and I-mean-business kitten heels and loafers. But this also makes it a seductive time to shop, so we need to have our wits about us.

articles.title: Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’
articles.summary: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to cleanup its mistakes rather than create original work. Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022.
body: By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down.
“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.

Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.

articles.title: ‘If he can make money in a tyranny, that’s fine by him’: Francis Fukuyama on Trump, democracy - and changing his mind
articles.summary: The political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy. Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to left.
body: There are not many public intellectuals who can say they’ve been cited by Capt James T Kirk of the Starship Enterprise, but Francis Fukuyama is one of them. In Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, William Shatner’s character is in a reflective mood, and speaks to the Klingon chancellor. “Some people think the future means the end of history,” Kirk muses. “Well, we haven’t run out of history quite yet.”

When the film came out in 1991 and in the years that followed, you’d often hear comments like that. They were nods to a thesis so famous it hardly needed spelling out. It debuted in a 15-page essay written by Fukuyama, then a 36-year-old thinktanker, which was published in the National Interest, a right-leaning journal of US foreign policy, in the summer of 1989. There was a question mark in the title: it was called The End of History?. In book form three years later, it became The End of History and the Last Man. But these were subtleties that, as we shall see, got lost.
points: The political thinker became famous for declaring the triumph of liberal democracy.
Thirty-seven years on, he explains what he really meant and why he made the rare journey from right to left.

Better year, however, is what all of these A-listers will be wearing on the step and repeat for the splashy premieres. This is, after all, the festival that last year offered the first glimpses of new-era Chanel, Dior, Versace and Bottega Veneta before their respective runway debuts, and which has given us Lady Gaga’s feathered Valentino couture gown in 2018 and Zendaya’s wet-look Balmain dress in 2021, among other standout moments.

articles.title: These Google Maps and Apple Maps Alternatives Still Call It ‘Lake Ontario’ (for Now)
articles.summary: Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The move was retaliation against Canada for walking away from contentious trade talks and in spite of the fact that Lake Ontario's name has nothing to do with the Canadian province.
body: If you live in the U.S., you may have opened Google Maps this past weekend to see that the app had already changed Lake Ontario's name. Even if you don't live in the U.S., you may see the name change: As it happens, there are now three different naming schemes for the lake in Google's navigation app. If you use the app in the U.S., you'll see "Lake America." If you use it in Canada, you'll see "Lake Ontario." If you use it anywhere else in the world, you'll see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)." Thanks, Google.

Whether you consider it basic bureaucratic compliance or corporate cowardice, Google Maps and Apple Maps now call the lake by its "new" name. It doesn't affect how the apps work (maybe unless you're looking for directions to, or information about, Lake Ontario), but if the change rankles you, you have other options: As it stands, there are now two key alternatives that still label it "Lake Ontario."

articles.title: Meet the Women Leading Norway’s Seaweed Revolution
articles.summary: Today, along the shores of Lofoten in northern Norway, a new wave of female seaweed farmers is redefining what has historically been a male-dominated profession.
body: It’s still dark as I pick my way down a rocky path toward the sea. The air is as cold as you’d expect from a Norwegian winter, but the wind is still—a small mercy as I peel off my robe and slide into my wetsuit. I’m preparing to dive. Not for fish, but for seaweed, a natural resource that is plentiful in this part of the world.

For centuries, the story of these wind-whipped northern shores has been told through the lens of the male-dominated fishing industry. But today, a seaweed-based movement led primarily by women is rapidly reshaping what it means to eat, farm and live sustainably.

Her enthusiasm is far from an isolated culinary quirk. As the UN warns we must cultivate the oceans to prevent food insecurity by 2050, these northern coasts are fast becoming a testing ground for a new ecological framework. Seaweed has a unique potential to scale sustainable, nutrient-dense food supplies, requiring no arable land, fresh water or synthetic fertilisers. It produces up to sixty percent of the world’s oxygen, absorbs dissolved nitrogen and captures carbon at rates that rival rainforests.

articles.title: This Bridal Designer Created Her Entire Wedding Wardrobe for Her Tropical Nuptials in Nevis
articles.summary: Designer Alexis Levan Whelan crafted four custom bridal looks—including her first-ever swimsuit design—to wear over the course of her destination wedding weekend in the Caribbean.
body: After years of creating custom bridal looks for clients, Alexis Nevan Whelan said there was “no doubt” she would design her wedding wardrobe herself. Her engagement to Cooper Davis came just after she began running her brand full-time, and she was fully prepared to create a lineup of looks for her own celebration. “I had done all that groundwork finding the best ateliers, finding the best factories, and finding all the best laces,” she says. “It was actually really beautiful to be engaged and go through that time with my clients.”

The wedding weekend would take place over three days on the island of Nevis in the Caribbean. The bride had a personal connection to the location as her aunt lived on the island and she visited with her family throughout her life. Alexis and Cooper knew it was a perfect fit for their wedding and began scouting venues for a full weekend of activities even before they got engaged. Those visits helped Alexis begin to ideate her looks. “I love designing with a location in mind,” says the designer. “It just feels so much better to me. I feel more comfortable and more confident when I'm in a space and my outfit makes sense.”
points: Designer Alexis Levan Whelan crafted four custom bridal looks—including her first-ever swimsuit design—to wear over the course of her destination wedding weekend in the Caribbean.

articles.title: 16 Hair Trends You’re About to See Everywhere in 2026
articles.summary: From hair jewelery to sculptural curls and graduated bobs, Vogue talks to the experts to find out the key hair trends you can expect to see everywhere in 2026.
body: The hair trends of 2026 have shifted toward specific moods: polished, with a genteel twist, and personalized. “Hair that is sleeker, healthy-looking and glossy will be big this year,” says celebrity hairstylist George Northwood. “Not hair that’s overly done or stiff, but styles that feel put together—with a natural, fluid feel.”

“There’s less emphasis on hair looking overly ‘done’ and more focus on movement, natural texture and small details that make a style feel individual,” adds celebrity hairstylist and Dyson Beauty global ambassador Irinel De León.

Think early noughties and ’90s elegance: crimped hair, crown braids, chignons, bouncy blow-dries, and rich brunette shades. These are looks that demand healthy hair and a more intentional approach to styling. While there are no hard rules when it comes to cut, color, or finish, the overarching mood marks a clear departure from recent years—which is precisely what makes it feel so fresh.
Below, Vogue speaks to the experts about the key hair trends that define 2026.
